challenges.name: progress-report-plan-quiz
challenges.title: Read the slow report's plan and check a rewrite
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the nightly progress report incident: the auto_explain plan of the report that ran for 40 minutes, and a first attempt at rewriting it with a join. Decide whether each statement is true or false.

questions.question:
The old challenge section of the same nightly report computed each learner's average best score with a subquery per row of report_learners, a work table the job fills first with one row per (learner, course). Part of its auto_explain plan (PostgreSQL 16):

->  Seq Scan on report_learners rl  (cost=0.00..46121488.30 rows=389114 width=16) (actual time=0.402..1117962.113 rows=389114 loops=1)
      SubPlan 1
        ->  Aggregate  (cost=118.43..118.44 rows=1 width=32) (actual time=2.871..2.871 rows=1 loops=389114)
              ->  Index Scan using submissions_user_id_idx on submissions s  (cost=0.43..118.40 rows=12 width=4) (actual time=0.214..2.862 rows=16 loops=389114)
                    Index Cond: (user_id = rl.user_id)
                    Filter: (course_id = rl.course_id)
                    Rows Removed by Filter: 41

Statement: "SubPlan 1 accounts for roughly 18 minutes of the run: its actual time is per loop, and it ran once for every (learner, course) row."
questions.explanation: True. In EXPLAIN ANALYZE, actual time and rows of a node are averages per loop, so the total is time x loops: 2.871 ms x 389,114 loops is about 1,117 seconds (18.6 minutes), which matches the 1,117,962 ms the Seq Scan above it reports. Each execution is a cheap index scan; what makes it expensive is that a correlated subquery runs again for every outer row. The misconception is to read 2.871 ms as the cost of the node and conclude the subquery is fast: always multiply by loops.

questions.question:
A first rewrite of the report's enrolled column. enrollments has UNIQUE (user_id, course_id), and lesson_progress has one row per (user_id, lesson_id) a learner has opened.

SELECT e.course_id,
       COUNT(*) AS enrolled
FROM enrollments AS e
JOIN lesson_progress AS lp
  ON lp.user_id = e.user_id AND lp.course_id = e.course_id
WHERE e.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY e.course_id
ORDER BY e.course_id;

Old report, course 7: enrolled = 2 (learner 1 opened 4 lessons, learner 2 opened 2 lessons).

Statement: "For course 7 this query also returns enrolled = 2, because the unique key allows only one enrollment per learner and course."
questions.explanation: False. The unique key limits enrollments, not the joined rows. The join produces one row per progress row of each learner, so course 7 gets 4 + 2 = 6 rows and COUNT(*) returns 6. The inner join also drops learners who have not opened any lesson, so the number can be too high and too low at once. Aggregate the child table to one row per (user, course) first, then join, or count the parent's key with COUNT(DISTINCT e.id). The misconception is that a unique key on the parent protects a count taken after a one-to-many join: it is the join that multiplies the rows (fan-out).

challenges.name: rewrite-progress-report
challenges.title: Rewrite the nightly progress report
challenges.description:
The nightly progress report of CodeDev ran for 40 minutes: it computes three numbers per course with correlated subqueries, one subquery run per course and, inside it, one per enrollment. Rewrite QUERY in the starter so it returns exactly the same rows but reads each table in one pass (CTEs, joins, GROUP BY). You may also add indexes in INDEXES (optional).

Tables: courses(id, title, category, created_at), lessons(id, course_id, position), users(id, email, created_at), enrollments(id, user_id, course_id, created_at, status) with UNIQUE (user_id, course_id) and status 'active', 'completed' or 'cancelled', lesson_progress(user_id, lesson_id, course_id, completed_at) with PRIMARY KEY (user_id, lesson_id); completed_at NULL means the lesson was opened but not finished.

Output: one row per course, every course (also one without enrollments or lessons), ORDER BY course id: [course_id, title, enrolled, completed_all, avg_completion_pct]. enrolled = enrollments of the course whose status is not 'cancelled' (the learners). completed_all = learners of the course whose number of lesson_progress rows for that course with completed_at NOT NULL equals the course's number of lessons; 0 for a course without lessons; do not use the status 'completed', which a separate job sets late. avg_completion_pct = ROUND(100.0 * (finished lessons of the course summed over its learners) / (enrolled * number of lessons), 1), the average of each learner's completion percentage rounded to 1 decimal place, 0.0 when the course has no learners or no lessons. Progress of cancelled enrollments and of users not enrolled in the course never counts.

The test runner (do not change) builds an in-memory SQLite database from each test case, either small tables or a generated dataset of about 200 courses, 3,000 users, 10,000 enrollments and 50,000 progress rows. It runs INDEXES (CREATE INDEX statements only, not counted), then checks the plan of QUERY with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN: a CORRELATED subquery is rejected as "too slow" because a report that reads every row must read each table once. Then it runs QUERY with a budget of 6,000,000 SQLite VM steps (set_progress_handler: steps are counted, not seconds, so the check is exact) and prints "too slow" with the plan when the budget is exceeded. Otherwise it prints the rows as a JSON list of lists, for example [[7, "Redis Patterns", 2, 1, 62.5]]. SQLite differs from PostgreSQL here: it has no EXPLAIN ANALYZE and shows a correlated subquery as CORRELATED SCALAR SUBQUERY where PostgreSQL shows a SubPlan; CTEs, LEFT JOIN, GROUP BY, CASE, COALESCE and aggregate FILTER work in both.
hints: Every subquery in the old report answers a question about one course or one learner. Which of those answers could you compute for all courses, or for all (user, course) pairs, in a single GROUP BY, and how small would that result be compared with the tables it reads?

Look at three places: the finished-lesson count per learner (one GROUP BY over lesson_progress with the completed_at filter, keyed by user and course), the lesson count per course (one GROUP BY over lessons), and the final join from courses, which must keep courses without learners or lessons (LEFT JOIN plus COALESCE). Count learners before you join anything that has several rows per learner, or the counts multiply.

The same shape on other tables: per category, the number of courses and how many have every lesson published. WITH lesson_totals AS (SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total, SUM(CASE WHEN published THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS published FROM lessons GROUP BY course_id) SELECT c.category, COUNT(*) AS courses, SUM(CASE WHEN lt.total > 0 AND lt.published = lt.total THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS fully_published FROM courses AS c LEFT JOIN lesson_totals AS lt ON lt.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.category ORDER BY c.category. The child table is reduced to one row per parent first, then joined once.
